about: One drawn, faceless composite person for each vicious cycle, so each cycle has a human thread. Each is a role, never a name or a real individual, and carries no figures of its own: the evidence for the cycle is on its page. Written in a careful, humble voice; shown with the note that it is a composite. Read by tools/build-static.js (/loops/) and tools/build-pages.js (/evidence-map/).
note: A composite, drawn from the evidence for this cycle. Not a real person.

people.who: A shop owner in a fast-growing city
people.story: The summers feel longer, so she buys a second air conditioner for the shop. It keeps her customers comfortable, and the power that runs it adds a little more to the warming that made her buy it.

people.who: A farmer on rain-fed land
people.story: After weeks without rain, the soil in his fields cracks and the afternoons feel hotter than they used to. Without moisture to cool it, the ground bakes faster each day, and the next dry spell starts sooner.

people.who: A herder high in the mountains
people.story: The snowfield her family has used for generations shrinks a little each year. The bare rock that replaces it holds the sun’s heat, and the edge of the ice retreats faster than she remembers.

people.who: A forest guard in the dry season
people.story: The undergrowth he walks through each morning is drier than it used to be. When a fire comes, it takes the trees that kept the valley cool, and the land beneath them dries out further.

people.who: A street vendor in a dense neighbourhood
people.story: Air conditioners hum above her stall, blowing their heat into the lane where she works. The hotter the lane gets, the more of them switch on, and the afternoon becomes harder to bear.

people.who: A water-pump operator on the city’s edge
people.story: During a heatwave the power fails, so the pumps stop and taps run dry. Meanwhile the power station upstream is short of water to cool itself, and the cuts come more often.

people.who: A smallholder with a borewell
people.story: As the fields dry, he pumps for longer each season. His neighbours do the same, the water table drops, and the well has to be dug deeper just to keep the crop alive.

people.who: A neighbourhood gardener
people.story: She waters the street trees she planted years ago, but a hot, dry summer still kills some of them. Without their shade the pavement heats up, and the trees that remain struggle even more.

people.who: A nurse at a primary health centre
people.story: On the hottest days the waiting room fills with people who are dizzy, vomiting or confused. With so many waiting, some are seen late, and by then their illness has become more serious.

people.who: A day-wage construction worker
people.story: He knows the midday sun is dangerous, but stopping means losing a day’s pay. When the heat makes him ill, he loses several days instead, and the next week he cannot afford to rest at all.

people.who: A family caring for a sick father
people.story: Treatment for heat illness costs more than they had saved, so they borrow. Repaying the loan means everyone works longer hours through the hot months, and someone else falls ill.

people.who: An older woman living alone
people.story: She has a fan but rations it to keep the electricity bill down. On a hot night she falls ill, the cost of care adds to what she owes, and next summer she can afford to run the fan even less.

people.who: A family newly arrived in the city
people.story: Pushed from their village by failed harvests, they rent a tin-roofed room that traps the heat. Illness costs them work, the rent falls behind, and they move again, to somewhere hotter and cheaper.

people.who: A girl in her early teens
people.story: When heat closes her school for weeks and money is tight at home, she starts helping her mother instead. She falls behind, and each year it becomes harder for her family to send her back.

people.who: A garment worker on night shifts
people.story: Her room never cools down, even after midnight, so she sleeps in short, restless stretches. Tired and anxious, she finds sleep harder to come by, and each night feels longer than the last.

people.who: A tenant near a new city park
people.story: The new park brings shade and cooler evenings to her street. It also brings higher rents, and she moves to a hotter part of the city with fewer trees than the one she left.

people.who: The owner of a small corner shop
people.story: In a long heatwave, customers stay indoors and sales fall, so she misses a loan repayment. The lender is more cautious next time, and she cannot borrow to buy a cooler or shade for the shop.

people.who: A wheat farmer before the harvest
people.story: A heatwave at the wrong moment shrinks the grain, and the harvest does not cover what he borrowed. With the loan still open, he buys less seed and fertiliser, and the next crop is more fragile.

people.who: A district health officer
people.story: She knows that heat played a part in many deaths this summer, but few were recorded that way. With so few counted, it is hard to make the case for next year’s heat budget.

people.who: A municipal budget officer
people.story: With money stretched, the cooling shelters and water points she planned are cut back. When the heatwave arrives, emergency spending takes even more of the budget, and prevention is cut again.

people.who: A small business owner seeking insurance
people.story: After several bad years, insurers no longer cover heat losses for businesses like hers. When a heatwave hits, she turns to public relief, which strains the budget meant for protection.
